entries.food_name: Muri (Puffed Rice — Famine Food and Identity Food)
entries.ingredients: Rice, salt for roasting, sand for heat distribution
entries.culinary_technology: Rice dried and roasted in dry sand in iron pan over high heat — rapid puffing by steam expansion. Result: lightweight, shelf-stable puffed rice. Can be stored for months. Eaten dry with salt and chillies, soaked in water (Panta variant), or mixed with jaggery/coconut.
entries.vessel_tool: Iron pan with dry sand, fine metal sieve
entries.scarcity: FAMINE FOOD: 'The experience of recurrent famines fostered a culture of food preservation and adaptability, exemplified by the widespread consumption of puffed rice (Muri).' (Mondal, 2026, Bankura food history study) Critical in Bankura's drought-prone laterite ecology.
entries.cultural_memory: 'Chalcolithic period to present — rice has remained central dietary staple for over three millennia.' (Mondal, 2026) Muri as post-famine adaptation — 3000 years of Rarh Bengal food resilience encoded in puffed grain.
entries.ritual_use: Offered to deity in various forms; Poha (flattened rice) and Muri at Lakshmi Puja and other festivals
entries.notes: Food history of Bankura from Chalcolithic to present — Mondal (2026). Famine-adaptive food technology. 'Muri' as most accessible food preservation technology in laterite Bengal.
entries.lost_traditions: Traditional sand-roasting technique being replaced by commercial machine puffing; quality and flavour diminished
entries.sacred_foods: Offered at multiple puja ceremonies in Bengal
entries.medicinal_value: Light and easily digestible; good for weak stomachs, fever; breakfast food
entries.cultural_significance: FAMINE HERITAGE FOOD: Bankura's laterite ecology + recurrent colonial famines created a culture of preservation. Muri = survival intelligence. One of most consumed foods in rural West Bengal across tribal and non-tribal communities.

origin.geographic_origin: Ancient South Asian tradition. 'Laja' (puffed rice) documented in Sanskrit texts from the Vedic period (c. 1500-500 BCE). Ritual use in Hindu marriage ceremony (Laja Homa) confirms its pre-Christian-era antiquity in India. Bankura's Kenjakura Muri Mela institutionalizes centuries of local cultural importance.
origin.origin_narrative:
ORIGIN — MURI AND THE ANCIENT PUFFED RICE TRADITION:

GLOBAL ANCIENT TRADITION:
— c. 6700 BCE: Popcorn (puffed maize) — archaeological evidence in New Mexico, USA (Native American)
— Ancient China (pre-1000 BCE): Popped millet documented
— Ancient India (Vedic period, c. 1500-500 BCE): 'Laja' (puffed rice) in Sanskrit texts; in Laja Homa marriage ritual bride offers puffed rice to sacred fire
— Ancient and medieval India: Puffed rice documented in multiple Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist contexts
ALL represent independent discovery of the same thermodynamic principle: rapid heating of grain causes internal steam to explode the grain outward.

INDIA-SPECIFIC ANCIENT ROOTS:
— Sanskrit name 'Laja' appears in the Mahabharata and other ancient texts
— Laja Homa (marriage ritual offering of puffed rice to fire) is documented across South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala)
— Puffed rice offered as prasad in temples from ancient times — connecting to ritual life
— 'In West Bengal there are various varieties made from different strains of rice — Kelas, Dahar nagra and Nalpai rice produce the best Muri' (Sourced Journeys, 2023) — traditional rice varietal knowledge encoded in Muri culture

BANKURA / RARH BENGAL FAMINE ADAPTATION: Mondal (2026) documents how Bankura's recurrent colonial-era famines (1770, 1783, 1866, 1943 are the major ones; multiple minor ones) fostered food preservation culture. Muri's properties — lightweight, no cooking fuel required, long shelf life (months), portable — made it the perfect famine survival and field labourer's food. The Kenjakura Muri Mela (annual festival in Bankura) represents institutionalized community celebration of this survival food.

TRIBAL INTEGRATION: Santal and Bhumij communities of Bankura coexisted with Bengal's broader rice culture for centuries. Muri was adopted as part of the broader Rarh Bengal food system, while the tribals maintained their own fermented rice traditions (Handia, fermented foods) alongside it.

CLASS POLITICS: Krishnendu Ray (NYU) documents Muri's class stigma among 'bhadrolok' Bengali upper caste — 'acceptable to eat on streets but had no place in refined cuisine.' For tribal communities, no such stigma existed — Muri was simply practical sustenance. This inversion reveals the political dimensions of food classification in Bengal.
origin.adoption_pathway: Ancient South Asian tradition predating any specific tribal community's migration. Santal and Bhumij communities of Bankura/Birbhum adopted Muri as part of integration into the broader Rarh Bengal food system, while the pan-Indian tradition was already present when their ancestors settled in the region.
origin.migration_contact: Not a migrant tradition — Muri is indigenous to the Bengal-Odisha zone and predates any specific migration event. Santal and Bhumij found it already present when they established in Bankura/Birbhum.
origin.timeline: c. 6700 BCE: Popcorn (puffed maize) archaeological evidence, USA. Vedic period (c. 1500-500 BCE): Laja in Sanskrit texts; Laja Homa ritual. 10th century CE: Pakhala (soaked rice) in Odisha — parallel ancient tradition. 1770, 1866, 1943: Bengal famines intensify Muri's famine-survival function. 2026: Mondal documents Muri as famine-adaptive food in Bankura food history.
origin.global_parallels: INDIA: Murmura (Hindi), Mamra (Gujarati), Mudhi (Odia), Pori (Tamil/Malayalam) — all regional names for puffed rice. GLOBAL: Chinese popped millet (pre-1000 BCE), Native American popcorn (6700+ years ago). COMMERCIAL: Kellogg's Rice Krispies (Western commercial version, 1927 — independent development of the same ancient technique).

entries.ecology: Dense forest ('bir' in Santali), kitchen garden ecosystem
entries.food_name: Moringa Oleifera (Drumstick Leaf) — Medicinal Daily Food
entries.ingredients: Moringa oleifera leaves; prepared as: soup, leaf mixed with pulses (dal), rice porridge (payash), or dried chutney
entries.culinary_technology: FOUR PREPARATION METHODS: (1) Soup — leaves boiled in water with salt and minimal spice. (2) Leaf mixed with dal — added to pulse preparation. (3) Rice porridge (payash) with drumstick leaves. (4) Dried leaves chutney — summer preparation: leaves sun-dried, packed in glass jar for year-round use. 'Santal women responsible for preserving leaves as source of food security.' (Murmu & Kannur, 2025)
entries.vessel_tool: Pot, glass jar for preservation, sun-drying surface
entries.season: Fresh: monsoon-post monsoon. Dried: preserved for summer use specifically.
entries.scarcity: Kitchen garden cultivation ensures year-round supply; dried Moringa bridges summer scarcity
entries.cultural_memory: SANTAL WOMEN AS NUTRITIONISTS: 'Santal women possess excellent knowledge in food processing and preservation to achieve adequate food supply.' Moringa as family nutritional insurance — women as planners and preservers.
entries.ritual_use: Not specifically ritual — daily medicinal food
entries.notes: Cross-border study (Jharkhand/WB Santal community). Four documented preparation methods. Women as primary knowledge keepers and food preservers.
entries.lost_traditions: Kitchen gardens declining as land is allocated for other purposes; Moringa drying tradition being lost to refrigeration convenience
entries.sacred_foods: None directly — but kitchen garden plants are spiritually protected
entries.medicinal_value: SUPERFOOD: Moringa oleifera leaves among the most nutrient-dense foods: Vitamin C (7x orange), Calcium (4x milk), Iron (3x spinach), Protein (2x yogurt), Potassium (3x banana). Anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic. Used in Santal traditional medicine for multiple conditions.
entries.cultural_significance: KITCHEN GARDEN AS FOOD PHARMACY: Santal women's kitchen garden = both food production and medicinal plant nursery. 'Santal tribal women are totally dependent on natural resources available in their vicinity and try to utilize indigenous methods.' Moringa = key species in this indigenous food pharmacy.

entries.medicinal_value: 15 species covering diverse medicinal applications — submitted to university for formal documentation
entries.cultural_significance: ETHNOBOTANICAL WEALTH: Santal kitchen garden = living ethnopharmacological repository. Women as primary knowledge holders of medicinal plant uses. Science is just now beginning to document what Santal women have always known.

entries.season: Seasonal variations observed between Kanhu (summer?) and Jhano (winter?) templates
entries.scarcity: Santal diet shows seasonal variation — templates show different nutritional profiles by season
entries.cultural_memory: Global validation of Santal food wisdom: 'The Santal diet demonstrated alignment with EAT-Lancet recommendations in aspects such as whole grains, starchy vegetables, vegetables, plant-based protein sources, unsaturated fats.' (Armes et al., 2024)
entries.ritual_use: Not specifically ritual — nutritional templates
entries.notes: GLOBAL SIGNIFICANCE: EAT-Lancet alignment. Two meal templates: Kanhu Thali and Jhano Thali. High protein from plant sources. NO dairy, NO animal protein. Seasonal nutritional variation documented. Published in Nutrients (MDPI, 2024).
entries.lost_traditions: Santal diet changing due to PDS rice/wheat dependency and market food access — the very diet being held up as global model is being abandoned
entries.medicinal_value: HIGH PROTEIN from plant sources; whole grains; diverse vegetables; nutritionally ALIGNED with global sustainable diet guidelines
entries.cultural_significance: GLOBAL VALIDATION: Santal traditional diet aligns with the EAT-Lancet Commission's recommendations for globally healthy AND sustainable diets. Indigenous wisdom validated by international nutritional science. Santal food = model for sustainable global diet.

entries.ecology: Junglemahal laterite soil, Sal forest, single paddy harvest ecology
entries.food_name: Sal Leaf Plates and Wild Mushroom (Seasonal Forest Foods)
entries.ingredients: Sal leaves (for plate-making and food wrapping), wild forest mushrooms
entries.culinary_technology: Sal leaves collected (peak: September-November) and used as plates/wrappers for food. Mushrooms (Chhatu) collected during late monsoon (June-September). Cooked simply — boiled, fried or as curry. Kendu leaves, Mahua flowers and seeds also major NTFPs: 39 plant species consumed as home food documented in Paschim Medinipur study.
entries.vessel_tool: Sal leaf plates (replaces ceramic/metal), bamboo basket
entries.season: Sal leaf: September-November peak. Mushroom: June-September.
entries.scarcity: Single paddy harvest region — forest NTFPs are critical dietary and income supplement for entire year
entries.cultural_memory: 113 plant species and 76 animal/bird species documented as NTFP use in Paschim Medinipur. 39 consumed at home as food, 47 for medicine. Forest = food pharmacy and food store.
entries.ritual_use: Sal leaves used in ritual food serving — food served on Sal leaf is sanctified
entries.notes: 113 plant + 76 animal NTFP species used in Paschim Medinipur. Of 120 surveyed households, 20% collect medicinal plants from forest. Commercial NTFPs: sal leaves, kendu leaves, sal gum, mushrooms, tubers.
entries.lost_traditions: Forest depletion directly reducing NTFP availability. 'Since the forest area was being depleting and reducing in size, they suggested planting of more trees.' — Shit & Pati (2012) respondents
entries.sacred_foods: Sal leaves used in ritual offering contexts across Junglemahal tribes
entries.medicinal_value: Wild mushrooms: rich in protein, B vitamins, immune-supporting. Sal seed: high fat, nutritional value.
entries.cultural_significance: NTFP = the invisible food system. The non-timber forest economy supports food security of an entire district. Its invisibility in policy means its loss is not counted as food loss.

entries.ecology: Junglemahal laterite, Sal forest, Mahua ecology
entries.food_name: Mahua Flowers and Seeds (NTFP Commercial/Food Dual Use)
entries.category: Wild Tree Product (Flowers and Seeds — Commercial + Food)
entries.ingredients: Mahua flowers (edible, sweet), Mahua seeds (pressed for oil — Mahua oil)
entries.culinary_technology: Flowers collected fresh in spring, eaten fresh or dried. Fermented for alcoholic beverage. Seeds pressed for Mahua oil (used in cooking, lamp fuel, soap). Both flowers and seeds are major commercial NTFP and home food.
entries.vessel_tool: Basket for collection, press for oil extraction
entries.season: Flower collection: February-April (spring); Seed collection: May-June
entries.scarcity: Major commercial NTFP providing income; flowers supplement food during lean season before harvest
entries.cultural_memory: Mahua tree = 'Kalpa Vriksha' (wish-granting tree) of tribal ecology. Every part useful — flower (food + alcohol), seed (oil), bark (medicine), leaf (plate). The tree that feeds without being destroyed.
entries.ritual_use: Sacred ritual significance across Santal, Lodha, Oraon, Bhumij, Kheria communities
entries.notes: Commercial NTFPs in Paschim Medinipur: sal leaves, Kendu leaves, SAL GUM, MUSHROOMS, and MAHUA (flowers + seeds). Cross-referenced with sacred Baha taboo (S-005) and Kheria nursery (K-002).
entries.lost_traditions: Mahua trees declining with deforestation; traditional collection rituals weakening; Baha conservation taboo no longer observed by some
entries.sacred_foods: Baha Puja requires collecting Mahua flowers ONLY after ritual conclusion — conservation disguised as sacred law
entries.medicinal_value: Mahua oil: cooking oil, skin conditioner. Flowers: high caloric value, sugars. Bark: anti-inflammatory.
entries.cultural_significance: Mahua tree connects Santal, Lodha, Oraon, Munda, Bhumij, Kheria communities through shared ritual-food use. Pan-tribal sacred food tree of West Bengal's forest communities.

entries.food_name: Gethi Kanda / Wild Tubers (Forest Margin Foraging)
entries.ingredients: Gethi Kanda (wild tuber), Bendo Sag (wild leafy vegetable)
entries.culinary_technology: Tubers dug from forest margins and forest floor. Boiled or cooked with minimal spice. Bendo Sag (wild leafy vegetable) collected alongside bamboo from forests. Poor households depend on these root vegetables as primary non-cereal food.
entries.season: Tubers: monsoon-winter (June-September collection). Leaves: monsoon season.
entries.scarcity: PRIMARY FOOD FOR POOR HOUSEHOLDS: 'Roots and edible leaves were collected from the forest, which were consumed by the poor households.' (Shit & Pati, 2012) — Forest as food safety net for BPL families.
entries.cultural_memory: The forest as emergency pantry: when paddy harvest fails or income is insufficient, tribal families turn to forest margins for roots and leaves. Knowledge of which wild plants are edible = survival knowledge.
entries.ritual_use: None — survival food
entries.notes: Specifically mentioned: Gethi Kanda (wild tuber) and Bendo Sag (wild green). Collected alongside bamboo and Kendu/Sal leaves. BPL household dependence documented.
entries.lost_traditions: Forest degradation removing wild tuber habitats; younger generation not learning tuber identification; women (primary foragers) increasingly in formal labour market
entries.medicinal_value: Wild yam tubers: carbohydrates, potassium, anti-inflammatory compounds
entries.cultural_significance: INVISIBLE FOOD SYSTEM: Forest wild tuber foraging is not recorded in any food census or nutrition survey — it happens in the 'informal economy of hunger.' Yet it prevents starvation for thousands of BPL tribal families in Paschim Medinipur.

entries.block_village: Karanga, Jhupo, Amdobe villages, Koniarya GP, Bagdah Block
entries.ecology: Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, Hooghly-Ichhamati river system, paddy delta ecology
entries.food_name: Arisa Roti / Chilka Roti (Munda Rice-Powder Bread)
entries.ingredients: Arisa Roti: ground powdered rice + sugar or jaggery. Chilka Roti: ground powdered rice (main dish).
entries.culinary_technology: Arisa Roti: rice ground to powder, mixed with sugar/jaggery, shaped and cooked. Chilka Roti: rice powder used as primary bread for main dish. Both are Munda traditions. Handiya (rice wine from fermented rice) distributed at festivals in leaf bowls (Dona).

entries.cultural_memory: Munda as 'Manki' — highly respected leaders before independence. Birsa Munda as prophet-warrior. Food traditions carry the dignity of this political history.
entries.ritual_use: Handiya (Bodoy/Hadia variant) is distributed village-wide in Dona (leaf bowls) at all festivals. 'Handiya is distributed among every man and woman of the village in a leaf bowl' — communal ritual.
entries.notes: North 24 Paraganas — geographically unusual Munda/Santal territory (Gangetic delta, not plateau). Cross-reference: Handiya with S-001 (Santal version) — same drink, different community name.
entries.lost_traditions: Commercial bread replacing Arisa Roti; market alcohol replacing home-brewed Handiya
entries.sacred_foods: Handiya offered to ancestors and gods at all ceremonies. Village-wide distribution = communal sacrament.
entries.medicinal_value: Rice bread: digestible carbohydrate. Handiya: fermented probiotic energy drink.
entries.cultural_significance: Munda food traditions: Arisa Roti and Handiya extend from West Bengal to Jharkhand as shared Munda cultural identity. North 24 Paraganas Munda = geographically isolated from main Munda areas but maintaining food traditions.

entries.culinary_technology: Millet fermented with traditional starter. Similar to Toto Eu but Lepcha variant. Consumed at social occasions.

entries.sacred_foods: At ritual occasions
entries.medicinal_value: Fermented probiotic beverage
entries.cultural_significance: Part of Sub-Himalayan millet beer continuum. Lepcha's Chhung = one link in the ancient Himalayan fermented beverage chain.

entries.ingredients: Maize (dhero porridge), wheat/maize flour (khapsa roti/bread), water, salt
entries.culinary_technology: Dhero: coarse maize flour boiled to thick porridge consistency. Khapsa: Job wheat (khapsa type) flatbread. Served with thukpa noodles or meat dishes.
entries.scarcity: High-altitude staple — provides calories in cold climate
entries.cultural_memory: Tamang as semi-nomadic people of Tibetan-Nepali origin. Dhero connects to high-altitude dietary needs where maize thrives.
entries.ritual_use: Festive food alongside Chhang beer
entries.notes: Tamang diet: Dhero/Thukpa + Maize/Rice/Wheat as cereals + all kinds of vegetables including chemo + Bamboo Shoot + Mushroom. Chhang, rice and Kodo beer for beverages.
entries.lost_traditions: Rice taking over from Dhero as primary carbohydrate; Khapsa bread declining
entries.sacred_foods: Chhang beer offered alongside at social occasions
entries.medicinal_value: Complex carbohydrates; high caloric density for cold climate
entries.cultural_significance: Dhero = comfort food of Darjeeling hills across communities. Tamang contribution to Darjeeling's food landscape — highland food in lowland context.

entries.ecology: Eastern Himalayan hills, high altitude glacier ecology
entries.ingredients: Corn, potatoes, radishes, kidney beans, beef/lamb/pork/yak meat (multiple options), onion, garlic, cumin, turmeric, chili pepper
entries.culinary_technology: Ingredients combined in one pot and slow-cooked as stew. 'Prepared with corn, potatoes, radishes, kidney beans, choice of meats, onion, garlic and spices such as cumin, turmeric and chili pepper.' (Aikat). Warming high-altitude stew.
entries.vessel_tool: Large iron or copper pot, slow fire
entries.season: Year-round; especially winter; important for warmth and calories in high altitude
entries.scarcity: Complete nutritional meal; meets high caloric needs of high-altitude mountain people
entries.cultural_memory: Sherpas = the people who carry the world's highest burdens. Phalghi = the stew that fuels the climbers. Food of extraordinary endurance.
entries.ritual_use: Served at festive occasions
entries.notes: Sherpa breakfast: Tibetan tea + Tsampa gruel. Lunch: boiled potatoes + sen (stiff grain dough with spice sauce). Dairy important: butter + curds. Chang beer at all social/festive occasions.
entries.lost_traditions: Yak meat becoming rare as yak herding declines; traditional recipes replaced by simpler modern versions
entries.sacred_foods: Chhang (Chang beer) has 'considerable symbolic and ritual significance in Sherpa society' — offered at social and festive occasions
entries.medicinal_value: Complete nutrition: protein (meat + beans), carbohydrate (corn + potato), antioxidants (turmeric), minerals
entries.cultural_significance: One of the most nutritionally complete single-pot dishes in the West Bengal tribal food archive. Sherpa food as high-performance food — the diet that enables climbing Himalayan peaks.

entries.ecology: Laterite Rarh Bengal, drought-prone, undulating laterite terrain
entries.scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor, Pennisetum glaucum, Eleusine coracana
entries.category: Drought-Resistant Grain Crops (Famine Food / Climate Adaptation)
entries.ingredients: Millet grains cooked as porridge, flatbread, or fermented beverage
entries.culinary_technology: Ground and cooked as porridge (similar to Dhero). Made into flatbread. Fermented for Handia/millet beer. Stored as grain for lean seasons — millets can be stored much longer than rice. 'Millets played an important role as drought-resistant crops' in Bankura's ecological history.
entries.vessel_tool: Grinding stone, iron pot, storage vessel
entries.scarcity: FAMINE FOOD: Millets are the last resort when rice crop fails. 'In scarcity, rice is replaced by wheat or inferior cereals like millets.' Cross-tribal: Santal, Oraon, Munda, Mech all use millets in scarcity.
entries.cultural_memory: FAMINE MEMORY: 'The experience of recurrent famines fostered a culture of food preservation and adaptability.' (Mondal, 2026) Millets = the grain that did not die in drought. Famine survivors taught their children: always plant millets as fallback. Oral transmission of ecological wisdom through food.
entries.ritual_use: Ragi (finger millet / Marua) is also fermented for Eu (Toto) — cross-ecological parallel
entries.notes: KEY POLICY NOTE: PDS system excludes millets despite climate crisis — tribal food heritage erased by policy. Cross-reference: Marua (Toto Eu base), Ragi (finger millet) = same species used by Toto for ceremonial drink. Same grain = different cultural context.
entries.lost_traditions: Millets marginalized in PDS (only rice and wheat available through ration system). 'Millets and pulses, once important components of the regional diet, have been marginalized as rice and wheat dominate public distribution systems.' (Mondal, 2026) — Policy actively erasing a climate-resilient food heritage.
entries.sacred_foods: None specifically — survival grain
entries.medicinal_value: Millets: high in iron (anti-anaemia), calcium, fibre; gluten-free; lower glycaemic index than rice. Climate-resilient and nutritionally superior to refined rice.
entries.cultural_significance: FAMINE HERITAGE: Bankura's food history is a chronicle of ecological adaptation. Millets = the survivors' grain. Three millennia of rice dominance could not erase millet's role as insurance crop. Modern revival of millets for climate resilience is a rediscovery of ancient tribal wisdom.

entries.ecology: Rarh Bengal laterite, Sal forest margins, temple town ecology
entries.ingredients: Wild honey from forest bee colonies
entries.culinary_technology: Collected from wild bee nests in Sal forest trees by experienced honey collectors. Honey used directly as food, sweetener, and medicine. Honey collection requires knowledge of bee species, nest location, and safe collection techniques.
entries.vessel_tool: Smoke torch for bee repulsion, clay pot for storage
entries.season: Spring (April-June) major honey season; secondary collection in autumn
entries.scarcity: Valuable NTFP providing income AND food supplement
entries.cultural_memory: Honey collectors as specialists — knowledge of forest bee ecology passed between generations. The beekeeper as forest knower. 'Wild honey and wax' listed as NTFP that Lodha people collect to sell (Sinha et al., 2020).
entries.ritual_use: Honey used in religious offerings and as sacred food in various traditions
entries.notes: Honey and wax = NTFP livelihood for Lodha (Sinha et al.) and Bankura forest communities (Shit & Pati). Listed as minor forest produce with livelihood significance.
entries.lost_traditions: Sal forest decline reducing wild bee habitats; honey collector knowledge not being transmitted; commercial honey replacing forest honey collection
entries.sacred_foods: Used in puja as offering; sweet offerings to deities
entries.medicinal_value: Antimicrobial, wound healing, anti-inflammatory; probiotic (raw wild honey contains diverse microbes). Cough, cold, wound treatment in indigenous medicine.
entries.cultural_significance: Honey collection = forest ecological knowledge in action. Bankura forest honey represents one of the most intimate forms of forest-food knowledge — knowing where bees nest across entire forest territories.

entries.block_village: New Mal, Matiali, Gayerkata, tea garden areas
entries.food_name: Kaloa Rice Khichdi with Vegetables and Dal (Oraon Daily Meal)
entries.local_name: Kaloa Rice Khichdi, Tahari Rice with Chicken
entries.ingredients: Kaloa rice (local aromatic variety), lentils/dal, vegetables (Lau/bottle gourd, Kumro/pumpkin, Mete Aloo, Man Kachu/taro, all leafy vegetables), chicken (optional)
entries.culinary_technology: Khichdi (rice-lentil blend) cooked together. Kaloa rice variety — local aromatic rice preferred by Oraon. Tahari rice: aromatic rice with chicken and minimal spice cooked together.
entries.scarcity: Daily meals
entries.cultural_memory: Kaloa rice = Oraon's preferred rice variety — distinct from mainstream Bengali rice preferences. Food choice as identity marker.
entries.ritual_use: Not specifically ritual — daily food
entries.notes: Oraon vegetable preferences: Lau, Kumro, Mete Aloo, Man Kachu and all leafy vegetables. Also eat: Beef, pork, mutton, all fish, chicken, duck, pigeons, fowl and even mice (rats). Broad food palette.
entries.lost_traditions: High-yielding variety rice replacing Kaloa and other local rice varieties; specific Oraon rice traditions eroding
entries.medicinal_value: Khichdi: easily digestible, complete protein when rice + lentil combined; traditionally used for illness recovery
entries.cultural_significance: Oraon's preference for Kaloa rice variety = indigenous seed sovereignty. Maintaining specific local rice cultivar as identity food.

entries.ingredients: Rice, tea leaves, fermentation starter
entries.culinary_technology: Unique Oraon variant: 'Hundi/Hariya, a liquor made from tea and rice' — incorporates tea leaves from the estate environment into traditional rice beer. The tea-plant habitat has influenced the fermented beverage culture.
entries.scarcity: Daily labour drink
entries.cultural_memory: The Oraon tea-estate worker who adds tea to their rice beer is both colonized and creative — using the colonial plantation crop to enhance their ancestral drink. Indigenous adaptation to a colonial landscape.
entries.ritual_use: All festivals and ceremonies
entries.notes: UNIQUE: Hundi/Hariya = rice beer made from TEA AND RICE. Only documented tea-inclusive tribal fermented beverage in India. Tea estate ecology directly shaping ancestral food traditions.
entries.lost_traditions: Tea-estate communities shrinking; traditional Hundi/Hariya recipe knowledge declining
entries.sacred_foods: Offered at festivals
entries.medicinal_value: Fermented rice: probiotic, carbohydrate. Tea: caffeine, antioxidants (catechins). Combined: unusual microbiome effect.
entries.cultural_significance: UNIQUE CULTURAL SYNTHESIS: Oraon Hundi incorporating tea = colonized community adapting colonial crop into ancestral food tradition. Subversive food creativity. No other tribal community in India documented using tea in their traditional beer.

entries.food_name: Panta Bhat / Khokora Bhat (Fermented Overnight Rice — Rajbanshi Breakfast)
entries.local_name: Panta Bhat, Khokora Bhat, Pontha Bhat
entries.ingredients: Previous night's cooked rice, water, salt
entries.culinary_technology: Previous night's rice soaked overnight. 'Khokora bhat or Pontha bhat' (Sanyal 1965, via Barman & Adhikary 2024). Eaten for morning breakfast before going to plough fields early morning. Isotonic properties — keeps agricultural workers hydrated.
entries.scarcity: Regular daily breakfast for agricultural workers
entries.cultural_memory: Rajbanshi men leave for ploughing before dawn. Panta Bhat = the food that waits for them when they return from first ploughing. Time-encoded food: eaten at specific moment in agricultural day.
entries.notes: Sanyal (1965): 'Rajbanshis take three big meals — firstly Puffed rice or flattened rice or Khokora bhat/Pontha bhat in morning...' Cross-reference with Santal (S-013) and Oraon isotonic baasi bhat research.
entries.lost_traditions: Commercial bread, biscuits and packaged snacks replacing traditional Panta Bhat breakfast in urban Rajbanshi communities
entries.medicinal_value: ISOTONIC: Fermented soaked rice = natural electrolyte drink. 'Baasi bhaat' studied in Oraon community as isotonic — same effect for Rajbanshi. Probiotic from overnight fermentation.
entries.cultural_significance: Cross-community breakfast: Santal (Panta Bhat), Oraon (Baasi Bhaat), Rajbanshi (Khokora Bhat/Pontha Bhat), Mech (Chura/Muri with tea) — all agricultural communities use overnight soaked rice as breakfast. Shared food wisdom across tribal and non-tribal communities.

entries.ingredients: Mentioned alongside Sidal, Chheka, Sukta, Shukati in Rajbanshi food canon
entries.culinary_technology: One of the key traditional Rajbanshi dishes mentioned by Sanyal (1965) in 'The Rajbansis of North Bengal' as important delicious food. 'Pelka, Sukta, Sidal, Shukati, Kachu Shak etc. were the important delicious food of this region.' (via Barman & Adhikary, 2024)
entries.scarcity: Traditional / special food
entries.cultural_memory: Part of Rajbanshi five-food canon documented since 1965 by Sanyal. Pre-dating the modern wave of ethnobotanical documentation.
entries.ritual_use: Possible traditional occasion food
entries.notes: Historic documentation (1965). One of Rajbanshi's core traditional foods alongside Sidal, Chheka, Sukta, Shukati. Full recipe documentation needed urgently.
entries.lost_traditions: Being lost — insufficient documentation remains
entries.sacred_foods: Possible
entries.medicinal_value: Not documented
entries.cultural_significance: Historic documentation — mentioned in 1965 as key traditional food, meaning it was already established in Rajbanshi cultural memory for generations before formal documentation.

entries.block_village: Jaigaon I-II, Dalshingpara GP, Kalchini Block
entries.ecology: Indo-Bhutan border, Jaigaon-Phuentsholing interface, Sub-Himalayan Dooars
entries.food_name: Cross-Border Meat Trade (Bhutan Saga Dawa / Alipurduar Abattoir Opportunity)
entries.local_name: Not a food item — economic food ecology
entries.ingredients: Pork (~12,000 pigs/year), beef (~1,200 tonnes Thimphu alone/year), multiple meats
entries.culinary_technology: Bhutan ALLOWS consumption but BANS animal slaughter within its borders. During Saga Dawa (4th month), all meat sale banned — causing pre-Saga Dawa hoarding. Alipurduar tribal communities in Jaigaon area supply meat to Bhutan. Need for modern abattoir documented — PPP mode or private enterprise with Ministry of Food Processing Industries grants.
entries.season: Year-round; Saga Dawa period creates demand spike just before ban
entries.scarcity: Creates unique market opportunity for West Bengal tribal meat producers; also creates consumption pressure during Saga Dawa — hoarding behavior
entries.cultural_memory: Bhutan's sacred month creates a cross-border food economics: Bhutan consumes Indian tribal community-raised meat for 11 months, then bans it for 1. The sacred law of one country becomes the livelihood opportunity of another.
entries.ritual_use: Saga Dawa = 4th month sacred period in Bhutan when meat sale/consumption is banned by National Assembly decree (2000)
entries.notes: Thimphu data: 1,200 MT imported beef, 1,000 MT pork (~12,000 pigs) annually (per Aikat source from AFRA Bhutan). Proposed abattoir site: Jaigaon I-II, Dalshingpara GP, Kalchini Block. Ministry of Food Processing Industries provides grants. Hashimara base and local demand also relevant.
entries.lost_traditions: Not applicable — ongoing economic dynamic
entries.sacred_foods: Bhutan's Saga Dawa ban = sacred law with food consequences. Animals are not killed in Bhutan but are killed and imported from India.
entries.medicinal_value: Not applicable — economic context
entries.cultural_significance: TRANS-NATIONAL FOOD POLITICS: Bhutan's Buddhist food purity law (no slaughter) creates economic demand that West Bengal's tribal communities near Jaigaon supply. Sacred law of one nation = livelihood economy of another's poorest communities.

entries.food_name: Lean Season Diet (August-October Food Scarcity Period)
entries.local_name: Tokta khabar (half-meal), Ek mukhor bhat (one meal)
entries.ingredients: Half-portions of rice, wild leaves, minimal vegetables — whatever can be gathered or afforded
entries.culinary_technology: Half-meals only twice a day. Some adults eat once a day. Wild leaves gathered from forest margins. PDS ration of 8 kg rice + 3.5 kg wheat insufficient for families eating rice three times daily.
entries.scarcity: 31% of 1000 surveyed tribal households face food scarcity in varying degrees (Pratichi Institute & Asiatic Society survey). 85.92% of Jhargram PVTG households food insecure (Dandapat et al., 2024). 7 people died in November 2018 — speculated food scarcity. Average death age 58 vs state average 70.
entries.cultural_memory: Hunger is not reported — it is hidden. Adivasi communities do not announce hunger; they reduce portions silently. 'Some adult members reportedly ate only once a day.' — the Pratichi Institute survey reveals what is unsaid.
entries.ritual_use: None — survival context
entries.notes: CRITICAL CRISIS DATA: 31% households with food scarcity (Pratichi). 85.92% food insecure in Jhargram PVTG (Dandapat). Scarcity months: Ashadh-Shravan-Bhadra (July-October). PDS insufficient: 8kg rice + 3.5kg wheat per person/month when families eat rice 3x/day.
entries.lost_traditions: Not applicable — this is an ongoing crisis
entries.medicinal_value: Deficient — insufficient protein, calories, micronutrients during scarcity period
entries.cultural_significance: CRISIS DOCUMENTATION: The August-October scarcity window = agricultural dead season (harvest not ready, previous year's food finished). This is when nutritional knowledge of wild plants becomes life-saving. The knowledge that PVTGs hold — wild tuber detoxification, forest leaf identification — is food security technology.

entries.food_name: Toto Oral Medicine Food Plants (17 Species for Dental Health)
entries.scientific_name: 17 plant species identified (5 in formal Codified Medicine)
entries.category: Medicinal Food Plants (Oral Hygiene / Dental Health)
entries.ingredients: 17 plant species used by Toto for oral hygiene: leaves, bark, twigs used for teeth cleaning, gum disease, toothache
entries.culinary_technology: Chewing plant parts (twigs, leaves) for antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. Some prepared as rinse/decoction. Direct use from forest.
entries.scarcity: No formal dental care access — forest plants are the only dental medicine
entries.cultural_memory: After deaths of Budhware Toto and Ganesh Toto (the last reliable 'Bai-Dangi' / Toto folk medicine men), only 16% of Toto families still use traditional medicine entirely. Traditional dental knowledge = among the fastest disappearing Toto knowledge systems.
entries.ritual_use: Not directly ritual — health maintenance
entries.notes: 17 plant species. 5 validated in formal medicine. 12 need urgent laboratory screening. Only 16% Toto families use traditional medicine — extinction threshold. Toto located: 89°20'E, 26°50'N, 8.084 sq km enclave.
entries.lost_traditions: CRITICAL EXTINCTION RISK: 'There is no reliable Bai-Dangi in the Toto society.' Traditional dental knowledge disappearing. 12 of 17 oral medicine plants not yet scientifically validated — risk of knowledge extinction before documentation.
entries.medicinal_value: 5 of 17 species validated in formal traditional medicine systems. Toto dental health plants: anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory. Common Toto dental issues: chronic periodontitis, dental caries, bad mouth odour, toothache, bleeding gums — from betel nut + Eu alcohol consumption.
entries.cultural_significance: MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE AT EXTINCTION RISK: With last traditional Bai-Dangi (medicine man) dead, and only 16% families still using traditional medicine, Toto's 17-plant oral health system is on the edge of complete knowledge extinction. 5 validated; 12 unvalidated but effective species may be lost before science studies them.

entries.food_name: Chhyar Pithe (Santal Version — Fermented Rice Cake)
entries.ingredients: Fermented rice, specific preparation technique
entries.culinary_technology: Traditional Santal fermented rice cake — Unit P-8 in RIDGGC Certificate Course. Taught as a practical cooking session. Specific technique not fully documented but involves fermented rice.
entries.scarcity: Special occasion
entries.cultural_memory: Part of the Santal pithe (rice cake) tradition — different varieties for different occasions
entries.ritual_use: Likely festival food
entries.notes: Listed as Unit P-8 in 8-practical-module course. First documentation in formal academic/educational context.
entries.lost_traditions: Fermented pithe preparation declining as non-fermented commercial alternatives available
entries.sacred_foods: Possible — fermented food as ritual offering
entries.medicinal_value: Probiotic through fermentation
entries.cultural_significance: Fermented pitha as distinct Santal category — fermented rice used for cake vs non-fermented. Shows sophistication of Santal rice food system.

entries.food_name: Summer Water Rice (Jol Bhat — Summer Santal Breakfast)
entries.ingredients: Cooked rice, water, salt
entries.culinary_technology: Rice cooked previous day. Water added (not overnight fermentation — fresh water addition). Eaten cold or at room temperature for breakfast with leafy vegetables, fish paste or dry fish.
entries.season: SUMMER SPECIFICALLY (Table 2, Paira & Ahmed 2025): 'Summer: Water Rice, Leafy Vegetables fry, Fish Stew/Paste, Boiled Vegetable Fry, Fried Mahua'
entries.scarcity: Summer cooling food — water rice as seasonal adaptation to heat
entries.cultural_memory: Summer diet wisdom: cooling foods for hot season. Panta Bhat = Santal summer intelligence — cooling, hydrating, requiring no cooking fuel.
entries.notes: Summer diet (Table 02): Water Rice + Leafy Vegetable Fry + Fish Stew/Paste + Boiled Veg Fry + Fried Mahua. Complete documented summer menu.
entries.lost_traditions: Being replaced by commercial packaged foods as summer snacks
entries.medicinal_value: Cooling, hydrating; fermentation (if overnight) = probiotic; helps manage summer heat stress
entries.cultural_significance: Seasonal food system: clear distinction between summer and winter Santal diets. 'Table 02: Summer foods' documented by Paira & Ahmed (2025) — rare detailed seasonal food documentation.

entries.food_name: Fried Mahua (Mahua Flower as Summer Breakfast Food)
entries.ingredients: Mahua flowers (fresh or dried), mustard oil, salt
entries.culinary_technology: Mahua flowers collected in spring. Fried in mustard oil with salt. Eaten as part of summer breakfast meal.
entries.season: SUMMER SPECIFICALLY: Listed as summer food in Paira & Ahmed (2025) seasonal table
entries.scarcity: Available in abundance during spring flowering — cheap, accessible
entries.cultural_memory: Fried Mahua = the taste of spring liberation. Baha Puja ends. Mahua collection begins. Mass gathering of flowers = community event. The fried flower = the reward for the long winter.
entries.ritual_use: Baha Puja taboo before collection; after Baha, fried Mahua = summer breakfast standard
entries.notes: Summer seasonal food (Table 02). Cross-reference: Baha Puja taboo (S-005). Mahua = connects Santal seasonal calendar, ritual law, and food practice in one flower.
entries.lost_traditions: Mahua tree populations declining; urban Santal communities losing access to fresh Mahua flowers
entries.sacred_foods: After Baha Puja = available for consumption. Pre-Baha = sacred prohibition.
entries.medicinal_value: Mahua flowers: high in sugars, fats, vitamin C; energy-dense natural food
entries.cultural_significance: Seasonal food as cultural time-marker. Fried Mahua = announcement of spring. The flower that signals season change through the kitchen.

entries.ecology: Chota Nagpur Plateau extension, degraded sal forest, nomadic range
entries.food_name: Wild Game Meat and Forest Produce (Birhor Hunter-Gatherer Diet)
entries.ingredients: Wild game (small animals, birds, rodents), forest tubers, wild fruits, honey
entries.culinary_technology: Traditional hunting with bows, nets, nooses. Roasted over open fire or boiled. Minimally processed wild food. Birhor = 'people of the forest' — most nomadic PVTG in WB.
entries.vessel_tool: Minimal — open fire, no fixed kitchen
entries.scarcity: Hunter-gatherer diet = entirely forest dependent; fully exposed to forest access restrictions
entries.cultural_memory: Birhor as the most vulnerable PVTG in WB — 'nutritional status of Toto tribe is comparatively better than Birhor and Lodha tribes' (Bisai & Dutta, 2021). Birhor nomadism = entire food system dependent on unobstructed forest movement.
entries.ritual_use: All significant hunts have ritual significance in Birhor tradition
entries.notes: Birhor PVTG: nutritional status WORST among WB tribes (worse than Toto and Lodha per Bisai). Forced sedentarization = food system collapse.
entries.lost_traditions: CRITICAL: Nomadic Birhor forced toward sedentarization. Traditional hunting completely prohibited by forest laws. Food system collapsing with nomadism. Nutritional status documented as worst among WB tribes.
entries.sacred_foods: First kill of hunt offered ritually
entries.medicinal_value: Diverse micronutrients from wild food diversity
entries.cultural_significance: Birhor represent the most extreme form of forest food dependency in WB tribal context. Their food system is a palimpsest of pre-agricultural knowledge.

entries.food_name: Winter Meat Curry and Pitha Feast (Seasonal Food System)
entries.local_name: Naram Mangsho / Sukri Mangsho (winter meat), Jel Pitha (winter cake)
entries.category: Seasonal Winter Feast Food (Complete Winter Menu)
entries.ingredients: Boiled rice, chapatti, dry fish paste/fry, burn fish, pitha (cookies/cakes), meat (per Table 02, Paira & Ahmed 2025)
entries.culinary_technology: Winter food calendar: Boiled rice + chapatti as staple, Dry fish paste/fry (preserved summer catch), Burn fish (whole roasted), Pitha (festive rice cakes/cookies), Meat curry. Winter = most resource-abundant season; post-harvest period enables festive food.
entries.vessel_tool: Multiple — iron skillet, fire, earthen pot
entries.season: WINTER SPECIFICALLY (Kartik-Agrahayan-Poush, October-January): 'Boiled Rice, Chapatti, Dry Fish Paste/Fry, Burn Fish, Pitha, Meat Rice' per Table 02
entries.scarcity: Post-harvest abundance — winter is the season of food prosperity for Santal
entries.cultural_memory: Winter = festival season. Harvest completed, storage full, community feasts begin. Laad Jel (truancy picnic tradition) historically peaks in monsoon but winter meat preparations are ceremonial.
entries.ritual_use: Multiple winter festivals: Sohrai, Baa-Parab. Pitha at winter celebrations.
entries.notes: Complete 4-season food calendar documented in Paira & Ahmed (2025): Summer, Rainy, Winter each with distinct menus. One of few seasonal food documentation studies in West Bengal tribal research.
entries.lost_traditions: Seasonal food patterns disrupted by year-round market access; winter specialness diminishing
entries.sacred_foods: Pitha and meat offered at winter festivals (Sohrai, Baa-Parab)
entries.medicinal_value: Complete winter nutrition: protein (meat), calcium (dry fish), carbohydrate (rice), fibre (vegetables)
entries.cultural_significance: Seasonal food calendar = ecological intelligence. Winter = abundance → feast. Summer = scarcity → Water Rice. The food calendar IS the ecological calendar.

entries.block_village: Mendabari Forest Village, Dakshin Mendabari, Kalchini
entries.ecology: Sub-Himalayan Dooars, rivers and streams, Indo-Mongoloid ecology
entries.food_name: Shedal and Bharta (Mech Fermented Fish and Paste)
entries.category: Fermented Fish (Mech Variant) and Roasted Vegetable Paste
entries.ingredients: Shedal: small dried fish fermented paste (similar to Rajbanshi Sidal). Bharta: roasted and mashed vegetables (brinjal, potato, or fish).
entries.culinary_technology: Shedal: dried fish fermented into paste — Mech variant of the widespread North Bengal fermented fish tradition. Bharta: vegetables or fish roasted in fire, skin peeled/removed, mashed with mustard oil, salt, green chilli. 'Taking of Shedal, Bharta are found among the Rabhas' — Mech parallel tradition.
entries.vessel_tool: Mortar for Shedal, open fire for Bharta roasting
entries.scarcity: Preserved fermented fish = lean season protein
entries.cultural_memory: North Bengal pan-tribal fermented fish tradition: Rajbanshi (Sidal) — Mech (Shedal) — Rabha (Shedal/Shedha) — all variants of the same core tradition. Cross-community food knowledge sharing across generations.
entries.ritual_use: Not specifically ritual
entries.notes: Mech also: Shrimp (favourite), Banana (preferred fruit), Christian Mech prefer buffalo/beef. Documented by Sanyal (1979) as first documentation of Mech food traditions.
entries.lost_traditions: Market dried fish replacing home-fermented Shedal; traditional fermentation knowledge declining among younger Mech
entries.sacred_foods: None documented
entries.medicinal_value: Fermented fish: calcium, B vitamins, omega-3; Bharta: vitamins from roasted vegetables
entries.cultural_significance: Shedal = Mech version of pan-North Bengal fermented fish tradition. Shows how a single food technology (fish fermentation) has been independently developed and named by adjacent communities (Rajbanshi, Mech, Rabha) in the same ecological zone.

entries.block_village: Dakshin Mendabari, Bhatkhawa Tea Garden, Kalchini C.D. Block
entries.food_name: Rabha Traditional Foods (Mairang Rice, Runchuo Puffed Rice, Konda Wild Potato)
entries.local_name: Mairang (rice), Runchuo (puffed rice/Muri), Khoi, Konda (jungle potato)
entries.category: Traditional Staple and Forest Supplement Foods
entries.ingredients: Mairang (Rabha name for rice variety), Runchuo (puffed rice), Konda (wild jungle potato variety), Pumpret (Khoi — popped grain), Shrimp, pork, mutton, chicken, duck, pigeon
entries.culinary_technology: Mairang rice: cooked standard. Runchuo/Pumpret: puffed/popped grain breakfast foods. Konda: wild jungle potato — collected from forest, boiled or roasted. Shrimp: caught from rivers by Rabha (who are 'good fish trappers').
entries.season: Year-round for staples; Konda by forest season
entries.scarcity: Rabha have good land cultivation and are 'good cultivators' — supplemented by forest Konda
entries.cultural_memory: Rabha as 'good fish trappers' — daily fish provision from rivers. 'Rabha and Mech are very good fish trappers so their daily dishes are served with good amount of fish regularly.' (Sanyal via Mallick & Basu)
entries.ritual_use: Choko/Fortica (Rabha rice beer) = ritual drink
entries.notes: LOST TRADITION: Chheka saag — 'which was once a staple food for the tribe. The modern culture has influenced them in such a way that they have let go of their old and indigenous traditions.' Direct loss documentation from field account (2025).
entries.lost_traditions: Chheka saag (wild leafy vegetable): 'The modern culture has influenced them in such a way that they have let go of their old and indigenous traditions and even food habits' . Chheka saag = LOST indigenous Rabha staple.
entries.sacred_foods: Choko/Fortica rice beer at social occasions
entries.medicinal_value: Wild jungle potato (Konda): carbohydrate, potassium
entries.cultural_significance: Rabha as 'absolutely pious and peaceful' tribe. Their food culture — abundant fish, good cultivation, forest supplements — reflects a balanced relationship with landscape. The Rabha food system = the most ecologically harmonious in Jalpaiguri district.

entries.food_name: Traditional Rice Varieties (Indigenous Cultivars Under Threat)
entries.local_name: Atab chal, Usha rice, Bhadoi rice, Heuti rice (Rajbanshi); Maibong/Inkhim (Mech); Kaloa rice (Oraon)
entries.category: Traditional Rice Cultivars (Genetic and Culinary Heritage)
entries.ingredients: Various traditional rice varieties with distinct preparation requirements
entries.culinary_technology: Atab chal (sun-dried, unboiled paddy): used for rice balls, Muri puffed rice, Chida flattened rice, Chalbhaja roasted rice, Payash porridge. Usha rice (boiled paddy): standard cooking. Bhadoi rice (winter paddy, hard to digest — preferred by field labourers for long energy). Heuti rice (rain paddy). Each variety has specific culinary application.
entries.vessel_tool: Specific to variety — different preparation equipment
entries.season: Seasonal varieties harvested at different times; Bhadoi = winter, Heuti = monsoon
entries.scarcity: Traditional variety knowledge = food security through diversity; monoculture = vulnerability
entries.cultural_memory: Rice variety names encode agricultural calendar: Bhadoi = harvested in Bhadra (August-September); Heuti = rain-variety. The variety name = the season. Ancient agricultural literacy embedded in food names.
entries.ritual_use: Atab (unboiled/sun-dried rice) used for ritual preparations — puja rice must be Atab
entries.notes: Rajbanshi rice varieties: Atab chal (unboiled sun-dried), Usha rice (boiled paddy), Bhadoi rice (winter paddy — hard), Heuti rice (rain paddy). These are pre-Green Revolution traditional landraces with distinct culinary properties. Atab = ritual-use rice.
entries.lost_traditions: CRITICAL LOSS: High-Yielding Variety (HYV) rice replacing traditional varieties. 'Indigenous rice cultivars, which were often more resilient to drought and pests, have been replaced.' (Mondal, 2026). Bhadoi, Heuti, Atab, Aloa — all under threat. Loss = permanent genetic extinction.
entries.sacred_foods: Atab chal (unboiled rice) = required for ritual offerings and puja in Rajbanshi and Bengali traditions. Must be unprocessed for ritual purity.
entries.medicinal_value: Traditional varieties: more complex carbohydrate profiles, higher micronutrient content than HYV rice; 'hard to digest' Bhadoi = slow-release energy for manual labour
entries.cultural_significance: SEED SOVEREIGNTY: Traditional rice varieties = genetic library of 3000 years of agricultural selection in Bengal. Each variety suited for specific ecology, season, use. Green Revolution has reduced this diversity to 2-3 HYV varieties.

entries.block_village: Binpur-II Block, Jhargram — hard-rock crystalline geological zone
entries.ecology: Rolling topography of Chhotonagpur Plateau, 40% tribal population, 13,694 ha forest (of 57,574 ha total), no suitable aquifer on NW side
entries.food_name: Jhargram PVTG Food Crisis Documentation (85.92% Food Insecure)
entries.local_name: Not a food item — crisis documentation
entries.ingredients: PDS rice and wheat (8kg rice + 3.5kg wheat/person/month — insufficient), wild supplements declining
entries.culinary_technology: Crisis diet: reduced portions, half-meals, one meal per day for some adults. Wild food supplements filling gap — but deforestation reducing wild food supply simultaneously. Double crisis: PDS insufficient + forest declining.
entries.season: Year-round insecurity; acute: August-October (Ashadh-Bhadra — lean season before harvest)
entries.scarcity: DOCUMENTED CRISIS: 85.92% of 855 villagers surveyed in 206 households = food insecure. BREAKDOWN: 33.98% mildly food insecure, 24.27% moderately food insecure, 27.67% severely food insecure. HFIAS measure applied (Dandapat et al., 2024). 48.19% undernourished (BMI <18.5). Children and women most malnourished.
entries.cultural_memory: The hard crystalline rock of NW Jhargram means no aquifer, no irrigation, no second harvest — the geological reality becomes the hunger reality. Nature and policy together create the trap.
entries.ritual_use: None — survival documentation
entries.notes: HFIAS methodology. 85.92% food insecure = among highest tribal food insecurity rates documented for any Indian district in peer-reviewed literature. Published in Global Social Welfare (Springer Nature, 2024). Key data: 48.19% BMI<18.5 (chronic energy deficiency).
entries.lost_traditions: The crisis CAUSES tradition loss: 'High WPR of 49% among Adivasis forces school-age children to work.' Children in fields = not learning food traditions from elders. Work poverty kills culinary knowledge transmission.
entries.medicinal_value: Severe deficiency: 43.48% men + 49.52% women undernourished. Children 0-18: 24.4% boys + 31.35% girls undernourished. Female working-age most affected (21.77%).
entries.cultural_significance: POLICY FAILURE DOCUMENTATION: 'Among all tribal communities, 85.92% have fallen into food insecure group.' (Dandapat et al., 2024). Formal SDG measurement applied to tribal PVTG context. This is not poverty — it is systematic exclusion. The food knowledge these communities hold (wild tuber detox, fermentation, NTFP gathering) is their only buffer against this crisis.

entries.food_name: Jel Lat / Mangsho Paturi (Santal Leaf-Wrapped Meat)
entries.ingredients: Meat (pork, mutton or chicken), rice powder, traditional spices, Sal leaves (for wrapping)
entries.culinary_technology: Meat marinated. Rice powder coating or stuffing. Wrapped tightly in Sal leaves (Paturi technique). Steamed or placed near fire to cook inside leaf wrapper. Sal leaf imparts distinct green forest aroma to meat.
entries.vessel_tool: Sal leaves (primary cooking vessel/wrapper), steam setup or fire
entries.scarcity: Festival food
entries.cultural_memory: Sal leaf = the Santal kitchen. Not just as plate but as cooking vessel. The forest technology continues: Laad Jel (hollow Sal branch), Jel Pitha (Sal-leaf steamed), Jel Lat/Paturi (Sal-leaf wrapped). Three distinct uses of Sal tree in Santal meat cooking.
entries.ritual_use: Festive ritual food — part of Santal ceremonial meat preparation tradition
entries.notes: Taught as Unit P-7 in Certificate Course alongside Laato Jel and Laad Jel. Completes the trinity of Santal Sal-based meat techniques: Laad Jel (hollow branch, bonfire), Jel Pitha (leaf-wrapped, skillet), Jel Lat (leaf-wrapped, steam/fire).
entries.lost_traditions: Sal forest access restrictions reducing availability of fresh Sal leaves; technique declining
entries.sacred_foods: Part of Santal festive meat offering tradition
entries.medicinal_value: Sal leaf adds tannins and trace minerals to the meat during cooking; aromatic compounds from leaf
entries.cultural_significance: Sal leaf as cooking technology — the ultimate forest-to-kitchen connection. Santal relationship to the Sal tree is not just ecological but culinary and sacred.

entries.food_name: Jel Sore / Mangsho Khichuri (Santal Meat Rice)
entries.ingredients: Rice, meat (pork/mutton/chicken), lentils/pulses, minimal spices
entries.culinary_technology: Rice cooked together with meat and lentils in one pot — Khichuri (rice-pulse-meat combination). Jel Sore = Santali name for this meat rice. Cooked in earthen pot for maximum flavour.
entries.scarcity: Festival food
entries.cultural_memory: Khichuri transcends communities — Bengali, Santal, Oraon all cook one-pot rice-lentil. But Santal Jel Sore includes meat and has distinctive spice profile.
entries.ritual_use: Community feast dish at tribal gatherings
entries.notes: Certificate Course Unit P-2: Jel Sore / Mangsho Khichuri. Taught alongside Jel Pitha (Unit P-3 and P-4).
entries.lost_traditions: Communal feast cooking traditions declining; individually prepared packaged food replacing community cooking
entries.sacred_foods: Possible community feast offering
entries.medicinal_value: Complete nutrition: rice (carb) + lentil (protein) + meat (complete protein, fat)
entries.cultural_significance: Cross-cultural convergence: Santal meat khichuri parallels Bengali non-vegetarian khichuri, yet maintains distinct identity as Jel Sore. Food convergence as cultural bridge.

entries.food_name: Pata Pithe / Shakam Pithe (Santal Leaf Cake / Dried Cake)
entries.ingredients: Rice powder, stuffing (not fully specified), leaves (Sal leaf wrapper)
entries.culinary_technology: Rice dough stuffed and wrapped in leaves (Pata = leaf). Shakam variant = dried/preserved pithe. Cooked in leaf wrapper by steaming or roasting.
entries.season: Festival seasons; Shakam variant can be stored for months
entries.scarcity: Shakam (dried) pithe = portable preserved festival food
entries.cultural_memory: Shakam Pithe = the preserved ancestor's cake. Dried to last weeks, the Shakam Pithe carries the festival forward into daily life.
entries.ritual_use: Festival food; offering at ceremonies
entries.notes: Certificate Course Unit P-1 — first practical session. 'Shakam' = dried/dehydrated in Santali. The preserved cake as portable festival food.
entries.lost_traditions: Drying and preservation technique declining; modern storage replacing traditional food preservation
entries.sacred_foods: Festival offering
entries.medicinal_value: Carbohydrate energy source
entries.cultural_significance: Two preservation technologies: fresh Pata Pithe (immediate consumption) and Shakam Pithe (dried preservation). Dual-form food = Santal food system flexibility.
